accounts.prose: Public package facade: it implements no merge logic itself, but wildcard-re-exports the runtime merge API, its `Merge` result type, and the array-concatenation helper. The facade therefore exposes `merge`, `mergeAndCompare`, `mergeAndConcat`, `concatArrays`, and `Merge`, delegating behavior to the merge and extension modules.

referent.description: the package entry module and its delegated public API

qualifications: Apparent functionality is inferred from captured TypeScript source and compiler-resolved exports; runtime execution was not observed.
The nearby README is treated as package documentation, not proof of behavior.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

qualifications: The merge engine delegates array-specific comparison to `concatArrays`.

qualifications: Plain-object, symbol, and array classification is delegated to the external `is-what` package; its implementation was not inspected.

accounts.prose: The exported `Merge` type predicts a left-to-right deep assignment for record-like inputs; otherwise it falls back to the last supplied type. `Assign` iterates the input tuple and delegates each pair to `MergeDeep`, which recursively combines record fields while distinguishing required and optional keys. `PrettyPrint` recursively expands the resulting intersections with a seen-type guard, while `List.Pop` supplies the last-type fallback.

referent.description: compile-time model behind the public Merge result type

qualifications: This is compile-time TypeScript behavior, not runtime merging.
The source documentation says `MergeDeep` needs strict null checking; compiler settings were not independently assessed.
The public functions cast their runtime reduction result to the computed `Merge` type, so correspondence is asserted rather than runtime-checked.

accounts.prose: The three public merge functions share one left-to-right reduction: each newcomer is merged into the result produced by the preceding step. For a plain-object newcomer, the engine constructs a fresh ordinary object, first retaining origin properties that the newcomer does not own and then processing every own property of the newcomer. Consequently, an unmatched nested object, array, or class instance is retained by reference rather than cloned. A non-plain top-level newcomer short-circuits the entire step and becomes that step’s result as-is; likewise, calling a public function with no newcomers leaves the initial value unchanged rather than cloning it.

The string key `__proto__` is skipped on both the retained-origin and incoming-property passes.

accounts.prose: For `mergeAndCompare`, the callback is part of assignment, not merely collision handling. It runs once for every incoming own property processed at every recursion level, even when the origin has no own value for that key; in that case its first argument is normally `undefined`. When both sides lead to recursive object merging, recursion happens first, and the parent-level callback then receives the original value plus the already-merged incoming-side result. The callback’s return value is what is finally assigned, so it may replace that recursively produced object. It is not called when a non-plain top-level newcomer triggers the early return.

accounts.prose: `mergeAndConcat` is not a separate traversal. accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: Both write branches produce ordinary data properties. The nonenumerable branch states all destination attributes explicitly and always makes the property writable and configurable. The enumerable branch uses assignment onto a newly accumulated plain object, which ordinarily creates an enumerable, writable, configurable data property. Consequently, a nonwritable or nonconfigurable source property loses those restrictions, and an accessor is replaced by the value obtained when the implementation reads it rather than by its getter/setter descriptor.

referent.description: descriptor attributes discarded except enumerability

qualifications: The enumerable-branch statement is bounded to this implementation's fresh plain-object accumulator and excludes the separately skipped `__proto__` key.

accounts.prose: When both operands own the same name or symbol, the origin-side copy is suppressed and the newcomer-side property is written, so the destination's enumerability for that key comes from the newcomer. With additional merge arguments, that rule is applied on each reduction step, allowing a later own property to change an earlier result property's enumerability. A nested recursive merge still writes the resulting nested value using the newcomer property's enumerability at the parent key.

referent.description: collision and later-source precedence for enumerability

qualifications: Precedence is based on membership in `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` or `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`, not on whether a property is enumerable.

accounts.prose: The implementation reads an origin property's value before checking whether the newcomer owns the same key. Therefore an origin getter can be invoked even when that origin property will be discarded because the newcomer replaces it; newcomer getters are likewise invoked when their values are processed. Getter side effects or exceptions are therefore observable merge hazards that are not conveyed by the simpler statement that one source property overwrites another.

It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: “Copies properties” here means all own string-named properties—including nonenumerable ones—and all own symbols are enumerated. Reading each property obtains its current value, so accessors are not preserved as accessors. The destination preserves only whether the property was enumerable: nonenumerable properties are recreated as writable and configurable data properties, while enumerable properties are installed by assignment. Thus complete descriptors such as getters, setters, read-only status, and nonconfigurability are not retained. The string key `__proto__` is skipped on both the retained-origin and incoming-property passes.

referent.description: property enumeration, descriptor handling, and prototype-poisoning guard in the merge implementation

qualifications: Property reads may invoke getters; that follows from the captured source’s indexed reads, but side effects were not tested.
The `__proto__` guard applies to that exact string key; symbols are not equal to it.

@investigram-945594d0 · interpretation
The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.
Referent: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants
  Qualification: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
  Qualification: Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
  Qualification: The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

The exported `Merge` type predicts a left-to-right deep assignment for record-like inputs; otherwise it falls back to the last supplied type. `Assign` iterates the input tuple and delegates each pair to `MergeDeep`, which recursively combines record fields while distinguishing required and optional keys. `PrettyPrint` recursively expands the resulting intersections with a seen-type guard, while `List.Pop` supplies the last-type fallback.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: When both operands own the same name or symbol, the origin-side copy is suppressed and the newcomer-side property is written, so the destination's enumerability for that key comes from the newcomer. With additional merge arguments, that rule is applied on each reduction step, allowing a later own property to change an earlier result property's enumerability. A nested recursive merge still writes the resulting nested value using the newcomer property's enumerability at the parent key.

@investigram-4f621241 · interpretation
The earlier account is accurate but incomplete: the merge implementation preserves only the enumerable/nonenumerable classification of each own property that is actually selected for output. It enumerates all own string names and symbols, reads the selected source value, and then materializes a new data property on a fresh plain-object result. Enumerable properties take the assignment branch; nonenumerable properties take `Object.defineProperty` with `enumerable: false`, `writable: true`, and `configurable: true`. Thus this is enumerability preservation coupled with descriptor normalization, not descriptor cloning. The repository README claims support for symbols and enumerable/nonenumerable properties, and the tests encode examples of both, but neither the documentation nor those tests establish preservation of accessors or of writable/configurable flags.

Both write branches produce ordinary data properties. The nonenumerable branch states all destination attributes explicitly and always makes the property writable and configurable. @investigram-004acbde · interpretation
When both operands own the same name or symbol, the origin-side copy is suppressed and the newcomer-side property is written, so the destination's enumerability for that key comes from the newcomer. With additional merge arguments, that rule is applied on each reduction step, allowing a later own property to change an earlier result property's enumerability. A nested recursive merge still writes the resulting nested value using the newcomer property's enumerability at the parent key.

  Qualification: This describes each merge step in the captured reducer and does not claim preservation of any other descriptor field.

@investigram-c93ceb35 · interpretation
The implementation reads an origin property's value before checking whether the newcomer owns the same key. Therefore an origin getter can be invoked even when that origin property will be discarded because the newcomer replaces it; newcomer getters are likewise invoked when their values are processed. Getter side effects or exceptions are therefore observable merge hazards that are not conveyed by the simpler statement that one source property overwrites another.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: “Copies properties” here means all own string-named properties—including nonenumerable ones—and all own symbols are enumerated. Reading each property obtains its current value, so accessors are not preserved as accessors. The destination preserves only whether the property was enumerable: nonenumerable properties are recreated as writable and configurable data properties, while enumerable properties are installed by assignment. Thus complete descriptors such as getters, setters, read-only status, and nonconfigurability are not retained. The string key `__proto__` is skipped on both the retained-origin and incoming-property passes.

referent.description: property enumeration, descriptor handling, and prototype-poisoning guard in the merge implementation

qualifications: Property reads may invoke getters; that follows from the captured source’s indexed reads, but side effects were not tested.
The `__proto__` guard applies to that exact string key; symbols are not equal to it.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

The string key `__proto__` is skipped on both the retained-origin and incoming-property passes.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.

accounts.prose: The exported `Merge` type predicts a left-to-right deep assignment for record-like inputs; otherwise it falls back to the last supplied type. `Assign` iterates the input tuple and delegates each pair to `MergeDeep`, which recursively combines record fields while distinguishing required and optional keys. `PrettyPrint` recursively expands the resulting intersections with a seen-type guard, while `List.Pop` supplies the last-type fallback.

qualifications: This is compile-time TypeScript behavior, not runtime merging.

accounts.prose: “Copies properties” here means all own string-named properties—including nonenumerable ones—and all own symbols are enumerated. Reading each property obtains its current value, so accessors are not preserved as accessors. The destination preserves only whether the property was enumerable: nonenumerable properties are recreated as writable and configurable data properties, while enumerable properties are installed by assignment. Thus complete descriptors such as getters, setters, read-only status, and nonconfigurability are not retained. The string key `__proto__` is skipped on both the retained-origin and incoming-property passes.

  Qualification: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: The three public merge functions share one left-to-right reduction: each newcomer is merged into the result produced by the preceding step. For a plain-object newcomer, the engine constructs a fresh ordinary object, first retaining origin properties that the newcomer does not own and then processing every own property of the newcomer. A property is recursively combined only when its incoming value is a plain object and the corresponding origin lookup is not `undefined`; otherwise the incoming value is assigned directly. Consequently, an unmatched nested object, array, or class instance is retained by reference rather than cloned. A non-plain top-level newcomer short-circuits the entire step and becomes that step’s result as-is; likewise, calling a public function with no newcomers leaves the initial value unchanged rather than cloning it.

Whether a value is a plain object, array, or symbol is determined by the external `is-what` dependency, whose implementation was not inspected.

accounts.prose: For `mergeAndCompare`, the callback is part of assignment, not merely collision handling. It runs once for every incoming own property processed at every recursion level, even when the origin has no own value for that key; in that case its first argument is normally `undefined`. When both sides lead to recursive object merging, recursion happens first, and the parent-level callback then receives the original value plus the already-merged incoming-side result. The callback’s return value is what is finally assigned, so it may replace that recursively produced object. It is not called when a non-plain top-level newcomer triggers the early return.

accounts.prose: `mergeAndConcat` is not a separate traversal. It uses the same callback machinery with `concatArrays`: an incoming array replaces a non-array origin, but two arrays produce `origin.concat(incoming)`. Because ordinary nested objects are recursively merged before their parent callback is applied, array concatenation still works at deeply nested properties while the surrounding object structure follows the normal merge rules.

referent.description: array-concatenating specialization of the common merge traversal

qualifications: Concatenation creates the array returned by JavaScript’s `concat`; elements themselves are not deep-cloned by this helper.

@investigram-0371ef29 · interpretation
The three public merge functions share one left-to-right reduction: each newcomer is merged into the result produced by the preceding step. For a plain-object newcomer, the engine constructs a fresh ordinary object, first retaining origin properties that the newcomer does not own and then processing every own property of the newcomer. A property is recursively combined only when its incoming value is a plain object and the corresponding origin lookup is not `undefined`; otherwise the incoming value is assigned directly. Consequently, an unmatched nested object, array, or class instance is retained by reference rather than cloned. A non-plain top-level newcomer short-circuits the entire step and becomes that step’s result as-is; likewise, calling a public function with no newcomers leaves the initial value unchanged rather than cloning it.

“Copies properties” here means all own string-named properties—including nonenumerable ones—and all own symbols are enumerated. Reading each property obtains its current value, so accessors are not preserved as accessors. The destination preserves only whether the property was enumerable: nonenumerable properties are recreated as writable and configurable data properties, while enumerable properties are installed by assignment. @investigram-9485db2e · interpretation
For `mergeAndCompare`, the callback is part of assignment, not merely collision handling. It runs once for every incoming own property processed at every recursion level, even when the origin has no own value for that key; in that case its first argument is normally `undefined`. When both sides lead to recursive object merging, recursion happens first, and the parent-level callback then receives the original value plus the already-merged incoming-side result. The callback’s return value is what is finally assigned, so it may replace that recursively produced object. It is not called when a non-plain top-level newcomer triggers the early return.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects are recursively combined; non-plain values—including arrays and class instances—replace the prior value. It copies own string and symbol properties, preserves enumerable versus nonenumerable status, skips `__proto__`, and leaves unmatched nested values by reference. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge; despite README wording about values being “overwritten,” the implementation also invokes it when no prior value exists. `mergeAndConcat` supplies the extension callback, which concatenates only when both values are arrays and otherwise returns the newcomer.

referent.description: runtime deep-merge engine and its callback-based variants

qualifications: The callback-on-new-properties observation comes from implementation; the README describes the callback more narrowly as triggering when a value is overwritten.
Copying properties materializes their values and preserves enumerability, but does not preserve complete property descriptors.
The README explicitly cautions that retained nested references can link results to inputs.
